headline: A DEA tip line for Mexico. Mexico calls it meddling.
summary: On Wednesday the head of the US Drug Enforcement Administration asked people in Mexico to send anonymous WhatsApp tips about criminals and corrupt officials. On Friday President Claudia Sheinbaum filed a formal complaint with the US Embassy and called it interference. A Sinaloa journalist sent a tip the first day and got a quick reply.

cover_question.q: Whose job is it to catch them?

cover_answer: Mexico says Mexico's. The DEA is taking tips anyway.
table_question: If the neighbors spot trouble at your house, should they call it in?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: A police team from the United States put up a phone number and asked people in Mexico, the country south of us, to send secret tips about criminals. Mexico's president said no thanks, that's our job. It's like the neighbors putting a lost-and-found box in your yard. The two countries are arguing in letters, and the grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: A phone number and a box in the wrong yard. The argument is between grown-ups, and it stays there.
5-7.why_long: A five-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, so the script hands them two objects: a phone number and a box in the wrong yard. Cartels and corruption never enter; the box carries the whole quarrel. Expect 'who's right?' Say the two countries disagree and are arguing in letters, which is what grown-ups do instead of fighting.

8-12.script: On Wednesday the DEA, the US drug police, posted a WhatsApp number for anonymous tips on criminals and crooked officials in Mexico. By Friday Mexico's president had filed a complaint: that's Mexico's job. Like a rival coach handing your players a number to report fouls.
8-12.why: A dated chain: post, tips, complaint. At this age they argue about whose rule applies, and this story is exactly that.
8-12.why_long: A child this age is working out jurisdiction without the word for it: whose rules apply on whose ground. The chain is dated, a post Wednesday, tips Thursday, a complaint Friday, and the coach from another team makes the reach familiar. Expect 'but what if the tips are true?' That is the journalist's point. Sheinbaum says it is her job.

13-17.script: If your own government won't catch the crooks, is it wrong to call someone else's? A Sinaloa journalist sent the DEA a tip on day one, fed up with narco-governments. Sheinbaum calls it interference, days after asking the US for a drone. Where does help become meddling?
13-17.why: Two true things: Mexico asked for a US drone, then complained about a US phone number. Let them find the line.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once, and this story hands them a pair: Mexico requested a US drone last weekend, and complained about a US phone number on Friday. The Sinaloa journalist gives sovereignty a face on the other side. Expect 'so is Sheinbaum a hypocrite?' Coordination and subordination is her distinction. Test it.

5-7.q: Is a tip line like telling on someone?
5-7.a: A bit. You tell someone who can help when you see something wrong. Mexico says those tips should go to Mexico's own helpers.

8-12.q: Whose job is it to catch them?
8-12.a: Mexico's president says Mexico's. The DEA is taking tips anyway.

8-12.q: Why is Mexico mad about a phone number?
8-12.a: Its president says catching crooks there is Mexico's job.

13-17.q: Is it wrong to call someone else's police?
13-17.a: Mexico's president says no. A Sinaloa journalist did it anyway.

13-17.q: Doesn't Mexico already work with the US?
13-17.a: Yes. Mexico asked the US for a drone last weekend.
